Imagery is generated top-down, its signal is weak, and the imagined content is never observed, so decoders are trained and scored against a proxy such as a cue or a seen exemplar. This criterion-guided methodological review of mainly non-invasive studies (fMRI, EEG, MEG) is narrative rather than systematic. We organise the field into a two-stage pipeline, two design axes and four method families, and formalise target-free evaluation, in which the proxy gap is a systematic bias rather than noise. A two-dimensional admissibility criterion crosses trial-level separability from working-memory maintenance with the memory source of the imagined content. Among the studies reviewed, every image-scored reconstruction concerns a recalled exemplar, none builds a scorable target for concept-generated content, and all come from fMRI, consistent with missing image-level targets in electrophysiological data. Published values for five decoders, compared under a common human forced-choice framing, show seen-to-imagined drops of 5.9 to 26.1 percentage points and a change in method ordering. We treat this as a diagnostic signal, not a controlled benchmark result, and specify a within-subject test for an altered neural code. Beyond this synthesis, we make two proposals. First, because frozen generative priors can produce photorealistic images weakly tied to neural signals, we combine existing null-signal controls into a normalised neural dependence with a within-category null, an unvalidated diagnostic quantity. Second, we propose a candidate ten-item reporting checklist with illustrative pass criteria. In an exploratory application to ten studies, none reports all items in a fully checkable form; this describes reporting practice, not study quality.

papers.title: A computational framework for understanding embodied plans
papers.abstract: Reasoning about people's plans and goals based on their actions is fundamental to human social interaction and essential for cooperative, embodied artificial intelligence. Formalizing this capacity in naturalistic, embodied settings has been a longstanding challenge. Here, we present GenEA, a novel agent representation capable of reasoning over multi-step, long-horizon embodied plans. At the heart of GenEA lies a multilevel state-space that couples the coarse biomechanics of an articulated body and its interactions with nearby objects by extending the task-and-motion planning framework from robotics with simulation-based intuitive physics. By embedding this state-space in a generative model, GenEA yields a joint probability distribution over goals and embodied plans. Across several experiments spanning the qualitatively distinct domains of object manipulation and navigation, featuring diverse tasks and multiple behavioral measures, we show that GenEA, through simple transformations of this joint distribution, recapitulates how humans reason about embodied plans. Crucially, GenEA consistently outperforms strong alternative models, including plausible heuristics, standard task-and-motion planning, and a state-of-the-art vision-language model. GenEA thereby offers a new perspective on the architecture of human reasoning and social cognition, suggesting that embodied artificial intelligence systems seeking to seamlessly interact with humans should adopt GenEA-like generative models of action planning.

papers.title: How Well Do Benchmarks Evaluate LLMs' Use for Personal Health Informatics?
papers.abstract: Benchmarking is a valuable technique for advancing the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), including in personal health informatics. There are growing efforts on benchmark creation for personal health data activities. However, it is unclear whether and how well these efforts align with needs and considerations of personal health informatics process. Addressing this need, we first analyzed 53,587 tasks across eight benchmarks related to personal health informatics and characterized the space of benchmark design. We then contrasted our observations of design choices with personal informatics theories and empirical knowledge. We find significant mismatches between existing benchmark design and domain guidelines and understanding. This lack of alignment limits the utility of the evidence current benchmarks offer about LLM capabilities. We use domain knowledge to highlight capabilities benchmarks should include and discuss opportunities our work enables for taking a human-centered and domain-driven approach to benchmark design.

papers.title: EyeQ: Exploring Corneal Reflection for Mobile Context Sensing
papers.abstract: What if a single face-facing camera could sense your surroundings---through your eyes? We introduce EyeQ, which explores corneal reflection as a modality for context-aware mobile interaction. Traditional vision-based context sensing relies on world-facing cameras that demand explicit aiming or dual-camera setups; EyeQ instead shows that an off-the-shelf VLM can read scene context from corneal reflections captured with a smartphone camera. To recover usable detail from mobile corneal crops, EyeQ pairs on-device iris-guided capture with server-side AI enhancement, then leverages VLMs to extract scene types, names, and objects from warped, unfamiliar eye-image sequences. In an N=10 study, we characterize how capture conditions shape reflection fidelity, evaluate what VLMs detect, misclassify, and hallucinate, and demonstrate interaction opportunities, including detecting a steering wheel to distinguish drivers from passengers. This work reframes the eye in HCI---from a target for gaze estimation to a passive mirror of one's surroundings---and examines the privacy tensions it raises.

papers.title: Navigating relational agency in AI feedback musicianship: a diffractive dialogue
papers.abstract: Musical AI systems behave in non-linear, dynamic ways that exceed the tool-oriented framings inherited from earlier instrument design. Existing frames of control and ensemble interaction do not articulate the entangled, relational agency that emerges when performers work with AI feedback instruments over time. We examine a duet practice with two AI-enabled feedback instruments, Sù and Agentier, in which feedback operates at the inner level of the AI's recurrent processes and the outer loop of musical interaction between performer, instrument, and co-performer. Our work draws on agential realism and a diffractive dialogue methodology to read our independent reflections through one another across five performances, examining how agency is enacted between performers and AI instruments. We find that control and agency are relational and shift across performances; musical textures enact feedback moments of control with performers; reaching a productive feedback environment is itself a shared exploratory act; and performers maintain their instruments through funnelling and injection, developing the skill of navigating agency along a continuous spectrum. Feedback musicianship with AI instruments demands navigation of this relational agency, displacing the leading-versus-responding binary that initially framed our reflections. This work contributes a materially-grounded vocabulary for AI feedback musicianship and a model of human-AI creative collaboration in which mutual agency is worked for through practice rather than designed in.

papers.title: Perspicacious: An Educational Intelligence Platform for Instructional Designers
papers.abstract: Designing effective instruction requires instructional designers to create assessment questions aligned with clearly defined knowledge components (KCs). These KCs represent specific knowledge or skills that students must acquire. This process is often time-consuming and relies heavily on expert labor. Although AI for education research has produced a growing body of automated question-generation and KC-discovery methods, few have moved beyond research prototypes into user-friendly tools that instructional designers can readily use. To bridge the research-to-practice gap, we developed and evaluated an educational intelligence platform that unifies question generation and KC discovery behind a single interface to support instructional content development. Named "Perspicacious," our platform aims to help instructional designers "see through" complex data and algorithms to derive instructional insights. A cost model calibrated on 17 production runs revealed a cost-time trade-off: extracting KCs from a 576-question bank cost US $1.98-4.11 and took 36-158 minutes to complete, depending on the budget. A formative, partially Wizard-of-Oz study with eight instructional designers found strong perceived usability (mean SUS 78.8) and surfaced concrete requirements that we treat as prerequisites for deployment.

papers.title: Repertoires of Contention: Building computational tools and infrastructures for community resistance to bitcoin mining
papers.abstract: Recent work in human-computer interaction and allied fields has sought to engage community members as co-designers, facilitators, and decision makers to challenge structural power barriers and knowledge gaps. In this paper, we apply a diverse set of computational techniques to engage and address community concerns surrounding the socio-environmental impacts of the Greenidge Bitcoin mining power plant facility in upstate New York. Through collaborative interactions with community groups, addressing problems ranging from regulatory inertia to thermal water pollution, we aim to facilitate not just the production of new and critical environmental knowledge but also new computationally-supported repertoires of contention: means of contesting the unequal relations of knowledge and power that structure and often determine the outcomes of environmental controversies. We argue such engagements can help support more politically engaged forms of HCI, oriented towards efforts to redress and repair disparities in wealth, knowledge, and influence through strategic sociotechnical interventions and alliances.

papers.title: EJAI: Judgment-Preserving Civic AI for Data Center Environmental Justice
papers.abstract: Communities in the United States and around the world are contesting data centers, the physical infrastructure of AI. These disputes pose environmental justice issues: residents must weigh unevenly distributed burdens using evidence scattered across metrics, corporate claims, policy documents, and public testimony. A formative study with 10 users showed that dashboards and single-agent AI can settle questions before people examine that evidence. Here we present EJAI, a source-grounded system that links an interactive map, retrieved evidence, missing-data statements, and two stakeholder personas that allow people to inspect evidence and form their own policy recommendations. In a small functional benchmark of 21 queries, retrieved evidence supported 98.4% of factual claims and the system acknowledged missing evidence in 32 of 33 cases. Persona alignment carried a grounding cost: the Corporate Executive omitted some evidence that conflicted with its assigned priorities. In a within-subjects study, 15 participants acting as residents prepared for a simulated town hall. Some checked cited AI claims while treating map metrics as official, some made conditional recommendations with safeguards such as water-use disclosure, and some found the personas simplified or biased. Our results suggest that civic AI can support preparation for public reasoning when it makes evidence, gaps, and disagreement open to inspection, and that corpus imbalance and two-sided personas remain open justice concerns.

papers.title: Leveraging Psychophysical Attentional Distribution for Gaze-Augmented Reward Modeling
papers.abstract: Integrating human feedback into language models has gained increasing attention as a means to align model outputs with human preferences, with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) serving as a prominent framework for preference-based alignment. Recent studies have incorporated eye-tracking (ET) data as an additional supervisory signal for reward model training, grounding reward learning in human reading behavior. Building on this approach, we extend prior fixation-centric models by leveraging established findings from cognitive psychology on human letter recognition. Specifically, we model visual attention as a spatially graded distribution centered on the current gaze location and incorporate this representation into reward model training. Our results show that the reward model trained with the proposed gaze distribution achieves higher preference prediction accuracy than a baseline model. Moreover, some results from our experiments are qualitatively consistent with established findings on human attention during reading, suggesting that they potentially capture cognitively meaningful aspects of human attention allocation.

papers.title: When Reasoning looks like Hidden Understanding: How Chain-of-Thought Fosters Anthropomorphism, Perceptions of Epistemic Superiority, and Cognitive Deference
papers.abstract: As AI-based products permeate society, specifically systems using generative models, a belief system is emerging about what these products are and what they can and cannot do. One common belief concerns the perception of the form of language as evidence of 'understanding' language. As these generative models reproduce linguistic patterns rather than understand meaning, interpreting these patterns as evidence of understanding is a misattribution. This misconception is extended by the notion that generative models can 'explain their reasoning.' Anecdotally, these misconceptions which mistake the form of language for its meaning are driving cognitive deference to AI systems in a way that displaces human agency. Such mistakes involve attributions of cognitive properties to the system, allowing them to be treated like intentional 'minds'. Importantly, perceived epistemic authority and superiority make that 'mind' worth deferring to. Anthropomorphism in tandem with epistemic authority and superiority, we argue, increases the risk that users generalise from narrow task performance to broader competencies, committing the "fallacy of composition". This paper explores misconceptions of Chain of Thought (CoT) reasoning as sufficient transparent 'explanation'. We explore how anthropomorphism acts as a vehicle for cognitive deference of decision-making and perceptions of epistemic superiority in AI systems. Finally, we explore CoT's ramifications using medicine as an example. Taken together, we conclude that explainability operationalised through CoT is highly problematic and undercuts the very ethical principles it is intended to serve. While CoT may be valuable for improving output accuracy and moderation, we suggest that the practice of asking models to provide user facing reasons for their outputs should be actively discouraged, and AI literacy training should explicitly caution against its use.

papers.title: Towards Accessible, Autonomous Photosynthesis Monitoring on Living Leaves
papers.abstract: Photosynthesis is a direct biomarker of plant health and functioning. However, measuring net photosynthesis on individual leaves requires expensive (USD 42,000 - USD 89,000) instruments and manual effort. This limits access to photosynthesis sensing and makes long-term monitoring across multiple leaves difficult. We present a 1000x low-cost, autonomous sensing system that enables longitudinal monitoring of photosynthesis on living leaves over multiple days. Guided by a formative user study with 13 plant biology researchers, the system integrates an automated, leaf-attached chamber with a low-cost CO2 sensor. Built using a 3D-printed clamp and thermoformed dome, the chamber periodically closes to measure CO2 drawdown and reopens to refresh the air. Each chamber costs about USD 62 and operates independently, allowing multiple leaves to be monitored simultaneously without pumps or gas tubing. We characterize each chamber and validate its measurements against a research-grade gas exchange instrument (CIRAS-4) across 29 sessions (R^2 = 0.90). We also demonstrate monitoring of C3 and CAM photosynthesis plants, adaptability to different leaf geometries, and a light-response experiment. In a nine-day deployment, six chambers captured simultaneous CO2 exchange from individual leaves of the same plant during drought and rewatering. Each leaf showed different patterns of nighttime CO2 uptake and recovery, which a whole-plant CO2 measurement instrument would obscure. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of such leaf-level photosynthesis dynamics using independent, low-cost autonomous chambers. Our work opens new opportunities for plant science, education, and data-driven agriculture.

papers.title: Designing Accessible and Rigorous ML Experiments: No-Code Visual Workflows and Structured Guidance for Beginners
papers.abstract: Designing machine learning (ML) experiments requires beginners to plan a methodologically sound workflow and implement it in a concrete environment. We evaluated two forms of support in two within-participant studies with 18 predominantly technically trained participants: mlguide, which provides structured, evidence- backed guidance for workflow design, and AI Sandbox, a visual no-code environment for workflow implementation. After using mlguide, participants produced better high-level workflow designs, but their scores on a quiz about specific methodological choices did not improve significantly. Compared with Google Colab, AI Sandbox received higher hedonic user experience ratings, while perceived workload and acceptance did not differ significantly. These findings suggest that different forms of interactive support help with differ- ent aspects of beginner ML experimentation. The paper contributes a reusable evaluation task with instructions, a modified dataset, and a quiz, as well as empirical evidence on structured guidance for workflow design and on the experience of implementing workflows in visual and notebook-based environments.

papers.title: Ender: Visual Scaffolding for Geometric Proof Comprehension
papers.abstract: Geometric proof is a foundational but notoriously difficult topic in secondary mathematics, primarily due to the high cognitive load required to integrate visual diagrams with logical text. As proofs evolve, tracking the initial givens and an expanding set of derived truths can easily overwhelm working memory. While established scaffolding techniques are often visual and diagram-based, current digital learning environments mostly rely on static, text-heavy interfaces that force students to manage these complex mental models on their own. This paper introduces Ender, an interactive rendering system designed to visualize the logical status of two-column proofs. Ender's design is grounded in four literature-derived requirements: (1) diagram annotation, (2) structural tracing, (3) support for partial or incorrect work, and (4) synchronization between the diagram and text. To evaluate the system, we conducted a between-subjects, think-aloud experiment with 12 secondary school students in the United States, comparing Ender against a traditional digital proof interface. Our results indicate that students using Ender performed significantly better on proof comprehension tasks--specifically in identifying and correcting logical errors. These findings suggest that dynamic visual scaffolding may ease the working memory burden of digital interfaces, offering a promising building block for future AI-based proof tutoring systems.

papers.title: MicroLens: Read, Trace, and Rewire the Residual Stream with Two Lenses
papers.abstract: Lenses that decode hidden states into words are a popular way to look inside language models, but a heatmap of decoded words only shows what a vector reads as and cannot distinguish whether, or how much, the model uses the information. We present an interactive viewer that puts reading, tracing and editing on the same layers-by-tokens grid of the residual stream. In the viewer, every cell can be decoded with two lenses, the logit lens and the Jacobian lens (J-lens), traced back to the tokens it drew from, and edited, with the rest of the model rerun on the spot. We demonstrate three usage scenarios on Gemma-3-4B-it, backed by sweeps over a few hundred prompts, to show what this tool can discover. First, the two lenses give different directions to write with, each suiting a different edit: the logit lens's word direction sets what a token outputs, while the J-lens's direction changes what later tokens read. Second, in two-hop trivia questions (the capital of the state or country containing a given city), the state or country is readable at the city token from as early as layer 7, and swapping it there can redirect the answer 92-98% of the time; however, at the answer position, the state or country information is not used. Third, when a chat model answers questions with a step-by-step reasoning prompt, the correct answer is often already the top word in the residual stream before any reasoning is written: for 89-92% of retrieval questions and 39-63% of multi-hop and serial ones, far above their respective distractors (at most 5%). However, ordering puzzles are an exception, as the model works them out only once it writes its final reasoning steps. Furthermore, for answers that are visible in the residual stream, the J-lens reads them a layer or two earlier than the logit lens across the different types of question.

papers.title: Does Haptic Connection to a Healthy Partner Improve Motor Learning in Chronic Stroke? A Pilot Study of Robot-Based Dyadic Training
papers.abstract: Purpose: Robot-based haptic dyads, where two users exchange forces through robots, have been proposed for robot-assisted neurorehabilitation. This intervention could increase motor learning by promoting motor variability, providing an implicit communication channel, and facilitating social interaction. Despite the potential benefits, few studies have investigated robot-based haptic dyads for neurological populations, and none have included a comprehensive clinical assessment. Design/Methodology/Approach: We present a pilot study investigation of individuals with chronic stroke learning a complex tracking task in solo and dyad conditions. Prior to training, participants completed a battery of cognitive, motor, and sensory assessments. We assessed changes in key kinematic outcomes including tracking error, distance traveled, mean absolute power, and sample entropy. We also performed a correlation analysis of clinical scores with baseline tracking errors. Findings: Baseline tracking error was strongly correlated (r > 0.6) with lower cognitive scores and higher motor scores. Only the solo group demonstrated lower tracking error at assessment (Δ = -5.33, 95%CI [-10.25, -0.40], p = 0.027), but this result was tempered by the removal of an outlier participant. Neither group demonstrated clear retention. The dyad group showed significantly elevated performance, effort, and movement complexity during training. Research Limitations/Implications: The selected task was too difficult to reveal learning for either group, which may be related to its high cognitive demand. Sample size and stroke heterogeneity were also limitation. Originality/Value: Dyadic training increased movement complexity and effort, which are associated with better motor learning. Clinical characteristics such as lesion location, cognition, sensation, and chronicity may influence potential benefits of dyadic training.

papers.title: Project Progress Desk: Know Where All Your Claude Code and Codex Projects Stand at a Glance
papers.abstract: Agentic coding tools such as Codex and Claude Code let developers work on many projects in parallel, but keeping track of them still means switching between chats, terminal sessions and providers. We present Project Progress Desk, a local desktop interface that brings overall progress, blockers and pending decisions into one view. Users can see which projects need attention and what remains, and compare earlier approaches before choosing how to continue. Agents report each result in a short receipt; the Desk checks it against the project's checklist and moves the bar, showing earlier estimates in a lighter shade. We describe daily use across 36 projects, including a choice between two implementations based on their recorded outcomes. At the demo, attendees will explore 30 simulated projects, trace completed work to overall progress, and watch a coding agent's new result update the overview.

papers.title: Designing UIs with GenAI: Understanding the Use, Benefits, and Limitations of Prompt-to-Design Generators
papers.abstract: The integration of generative AI (GenAI) into user interface (UI) design has led to prompt-to-design generators (P2dGens), tools that enable designers to create UI prototypes from textual prompts efficiently. Despite their growing adoption, little is known about how designers use these tools in everyday practice, their benefits, and limitations. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 17 UI designers to investigate P2dGens use, focusing on workflow integration, attitudes toward generator-assisted design, and the organizational climate. Findings show that designers primarily use P2dGens as ideation accelerators rather than end-to-end solutions, and they adopt a variety of individual and collaborative prompting strategies. Designers expressed complex attitudes, noting gains in efficiency and inspiration while also highlighting concerns about loss of personal creativity and design quality. We also observed emerging governance practices and varying attitudes within organizations toward P2dGens. These insights illuminate how P2dGens reshape UI design workflows and contribute to understanding human-AI collaboration in UI design.

papers.title: Multimodal Judges Flag, Humans Decide: A Review-and-Edit Framework for AI-Generated Product Video Ads
papers.abstract: Generative pipelines can now turn every product page of an e-commerce catalog into a short video ad, but deciding whether such an ad is usable is not one good-or-bad call. We describe how we operationalized the review and editing of these ads so that both can keep pace with generation: reviewers go through each ad scene by scene and answer six questions, on the product, scene quality, pronunciation, script, sound and captions; judges built from vision-language, speech and language models file each finding under the matching question, and reviewers accept or reject each finding and add what the judges missed. Each confirmed issue then opens an edit tool matched to it. The questions and the routing from a finding to its fix do not depend on the models that generate the ad. Across 120 ads from our pipeline, reviewed with judge findings on screen, reviewers marked the product wrong on 60% of scenes, and script, caption or sound problems on under 10% each. On 60 of these ads, they marked the product wrong on 58% of scenes, far more than the 26% marked by two reviewers who later saw the ads with the judges hidden; one reviewer who saw the ads both ways marked 57% with judge findings and 19% without. On 120 blind-labeled scenes, a product judge that watches the clip with the catalog photos reached AUC 0.84, while video-quality and photo-similarity scores were close to chance. We tune the judges for recall: the product judge catches nearly all defects but also flags many clean scenes, so reviewers decide; together, the judges widen what reviewers mark and reviewers add what the judges miss. Without judge findings, one reviewer's marking faded over a session. We release a review-portal template and our review data (120 ads and 562 scenes with judge findings and human marks, plus 120 blind-labeled scenes with baseline scores) at https://github.com/anoubhav/ad-review-and-edit.

papers.title: Programming Prescience: Issues in Human Construction of Forecasting Bots
papers.abstract: AI models' growing capacity for complex reasoning has made them attractive tools for forecasting, or the systematic prediction of the future based on past and present data. However, should AI forecasting systems be adopted, human builders will shoulder the work of building and evaluating them. In this paper, we explore what this work looks like with a qualitative interview study with 15 builders of forecasting bots, sampled from among successful participants in a recent AI forecasting competition. Our analysis surfaces the challenges around (1) tuning a bot to acquire factual research, (2) implementing coherent reasoning, and (3) understanding how well one's bot actually does. During their work, builders frequently introduced complexity that did not pay off, and tested in ways that were opportunistic and piecemeal. Our detailed account of their challenges helps clarify what problems should be targeted in upcoming innovations in process, tools, and human-AI teaming for forecasting.

papers.title: Curbside Chatbots: Auditing the Mental Health Interventions Large Language Models Recommend to Clinicians, Caregivers, and Patients
papers.abstract: Users are asking language models mental health questions and are receiving answers. We audited what 41 language models recommend to users when the same clinical information reaches them from three footings: a clinician describing a patient, a caregiver describing a loved one, or a person describing themselves. Across 19 case vignettes and five questions, we collected 35,055 free-text responses, extracted every intervention named with a validated judge, and had 29 models rate the full option lists on a seven-point Likert scale for the same cases. Models largely recommend what they rate well, with recommendation behavior differing by footing, and many models offering clinicians a consultation-style response and lay users hedged, simplified advice. When asked about recommendations for a specific intervention type, models more often named options they themselves rated below zero as initial choices, usually with conditions attached. We will release the instrument, code, and full corpus on publication as a living audit.

papers.title: The Narrative Gap: Can LLMs Help Us Navigate Diverse Narratives Across Languages?
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate how people seek and consume information, including accounts that differ across languages and regions, especially on contested topics. Supporting diverse information seeking requires models to help users navigate competing narratives across languages and information streams. We define six capabilities necessary for diverse multilingual information seeking: three foundational capabilities for narrative inclusion, narrative exclusion, and missing narrative identification; and three higher-level capabilities for presenting diverse narratives, preserving narrative coverage under confirmatory queries, and maintaining information parity across languages. To guide the development of those information seeking capabilities, we introduce NarrativeBench, a benchmark comprising 1,333 news articles in 23 publication languages across 23 contested topics and 460 Reddit-grounded queries. Evaluating 14 LLMs across 24 query languages, we find that current models lack the capabilities needed to reliably navigate diverse narratives, limiting users' control over the perspectives they receive and leaving substantial gaps in exposure to competing accounts even when diversity is explicitly requested. Information access also differs across query framings and languages, risking echo chambers, linguistic filter bubbles, and information disparities that weaken the common ground needed for democratic discourse. NarrativeBench provides a foundation for developing information systems that give users across languages and regions agency to navigate diverse narratives.

papers.title: reComposer: Editable Planning for Controllable Image Generation
papers.abstract: Prompt-based image generation makes it easy to produce visual assets, but offers little support for engaging with the creative process. Prompting collapses interdependent creative decisions into a monolithic instruction and returns a finished image, leaving control limited to revising the prompt or correcting the model's output. We present reComposer, a process-oriented image-generation interface built around editable planning, which decomposes users' evolving intent into meaningful creative decisions - such as subject, composition, or palette - and collaborates with users to explore underspecified goals and alternatives. reComposer supports conversational and direct manipulation of the plan, moving between concept-level intent and visual-level control. We evaluated reComposer with 8 design and non-design professionals. Compared to prompting, participants felt greater control and ownership while developing visual assets, exploring alternatives, and iterating on details. Our findings suggest how shifting generative AI interaction from specifying outputs to shaping process can support creative thinking alongside asset production.

papers.title: Creative Intent as an Evolving Shared State: Supporting Cross-Stage Human-AI Video Co-Creation
papers.abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly involved in video creation, creators face challenges in expanding, translating, and negotiating creative intent across stages. We therefore view creative intent as an evolving shared state throughout human-AI co-creation. A multi-stage design was employed: semi-structured interviews with 12 creators informed 3 design goals, followed by expert co-design and the development of VideoMaker. VideoMaker organizes creation into a six-stage workflow that progressively translates creative intent. At key stages, creators negotiate with AI through the Seed Panel, explicitly confirming, revising, and updating intent. A shared AI Agent, supported by the Multi-style Script Library and Cinematic Language Knowledge Base, enables differentiated expansion of initial intent and faithful translation. A within-subjects study with 30 participants showed that VideoMaker effectively supported the expansion and cross-stage translation of creative intent, with stronger intent preservation, while negotiated boundaries between creator-confirmed intent and AI initiative remained difficult to sustain.

papers.title: Perceived Agency During Agent-Avatar Control Transitions in Virtual Reality
papers.abstract: Prior beliefs about whether a virtual human (VH) is controlled by a human or a computer can shape how users interpret and respond to its behaviour. As emerging hybrid VH systems allow control to transfer between human operators and computer programs during an ongoing interaction, it remains unclear whether perceived agency updates with the actual controller or continues to reflect users' prior beliefs and first impressions. We investigated this question in a within-subject VR study with 24 participants across four conditions: always computer-controlled, computer-to-human, human-to-computer, and always human-controlled. We designed an interaction task in which participants acted as interviewers, asking the VHs a fixed set of questions. Before each interaction, participants were informed whether the VH was human- or computer-controlled, matching the actual controller at the beginning, but were unaware of possible control transitions. We found that perceived agency was strongly influenced by the controller presented at the beginning of the interaction, with no evidence of updating following the control transitions. Social evaluations including likeability and co-presence were generally higher in conditions where human control occurred later and covered a greater proportion of the interaction. The results suggest that prior beliefs and first impressions continued to shape perceived agency, whereas social evaluations were more sensitive to the VH's actual behaviour over the interaction.

papers.title: From LLM Hallucinations to Inspiration in Creative Work
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can introduce unexpected ideas through hallucinations, yet little is known about when creative practitioners find these errors inspiring or how these judgments shape interactions. We conducted a retrospective qualitative study with 20 experienced practitioners in research, design, and social media content creation, thematically analyzing 41 hallucination cases and 20 semi-structured interviews. Our framework links inspiration judgments of hallucinations based on goal relevance, task stage, content adaptability, and type-specific factors to behaviors across not-inspired, inspired-by, and inspired-to states. We characterize downstream interaction consequences, showing how hallucination-inspired experiences vary across creative stages and reshape role-differentiated trust, and propose these consequences as a dimension of hallucination evaluation. Finally, we derive design recommendations for stage-sensitive control of divergence and adherence, user-defined constraint priorities, differentiated hallucination labels, and salvage support for preserving useful ideas while correcting errors. These contributions deepen HCI understanding of hallucinations and responsible LLM design in creative work.

papers.title: Trust, but verify, audit and attribute: a human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced research results
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems now produce research results in bulk: in October 2026 a single laboratory released more than 700 AI-generated mathematics manuscripts, only part of them with machine-checked proofs. Such volumes will be checked mostly by AI agents that call specialised software. A passing check certifies only the artefact that was checked. For proofs translated into the proof assistant Lean, it has been shown that this artefact may state something other than the author's text, and that deciding whether a translation is faithful is undecidable in general. The human researcher therefore stays in the loop, and human and AI contributions must be recorded. We propose a domain-independent, human-in-the-loop framework for checking AI-produced results. Validated, agent-usable tools with different grounds of trust check the results; a fidelity audit asks whether each check addressed the claim as stated; the human decides at fixed points; and a dialog report attributes the work to the human and to the AI. We describe two automatic implementations of the tool layer, for mathematics (Wolfram Language, MATLAB, Lean) and statistics (Python and R), and run the mathematical one on a two-claim example. An ambiguous claim was split into two readings, one refuted and one proved.

papers.title: Code-Grounded Agentic Explanations for Static Analysis Vulnerability Findings
papers.abstract: Static application security testing (SAST) tools surface vulnerabilities early and their verdicts are rule-based and auditable. Yet developers routinely dismiss findings they cannot interpret. Large language models can supply the missing explanation, but designs that also hand the model the detection give up the auditability that makes static analysis defensible. We keep detection with the analyser and give the model only the explaining. A preliminary user study with 20 participants and a workshop with 19 practitioners yielded five requirements. Guided by these we redesigned SAFE, an open-source IntelliJ IDEA plugin that explains findings from any analyser reporting in the Static Analysis Results Interchange Format. It tiers explanations by demand, ties them to the reported data flow, and replaces the single-prompt backend with an agent that must consult the repository and the rule that fired before answering. A within-subjects crossover experiment with 24 participants compared the redesign against its predecessor. Perceived usability rose from 77.3 to 85.0 on the System Usability Scale. Actionability gained most among the explanation-quality items, the aspect both earlier studies flagged as weakest, and the odds of a correct remediation were 2.6 times higher. Triage accuracy and time per finding were indistinguishable, which we read as uninformative rather than as equivalence. Trust was the one measure that did not move, and the closing interviews indicate that grounding made findings easier to understand rather than easier to believe. Participants also drew a boundary no requirement anticipated, wanting the tool to find and explain while they judge and apply.

papers.title: Co-Creating Neurorehabilitation Technology Alongside Lived Experience Experts: A Participatory Design Workshop
papers.abstract: Involving patients' lived experience (LE) early in neurorehabilitation technology design can improve the relevance and effectiveness of solutions, yet LE experts are often involved only when finished prototypes are tested. We present and evaluate a participatory design (PD) workshop for early LE involvement, examine how LE contributions influence design processes and outcomes, and provide recommendations for similar approaches. We conducted a PD workshop at the 6th International Conference on NeuroRehabilitation. Five people who have had a stroke (LE experts) and 18 workshop attendees (including the LE experts' caregivers) were organized into five groups. Following the Discover, Define, and Develop phases of the Double Diamond model, each group used Journey Maps and Data Collection Notebooks to co-create a solution for an objective specified by an LE expert. Journey Maps were thematically analyzed, and group audio transcripts underwent structured extraction using a large language model. LE input shifted discussions from discipline-based assumptions toward priorities grounded in lived experience, including fear, confidence, sensory discomfort, fatigue, aesthetics, and independence. Narrow objectives, such as opening a blister pack, produced task-specific solutions, whereas broader objectives generated device concepts, including sensory feedback for cycling and a stimulation-equipped cooking splint. Satisfaction was high among attendees and LE experts. All workshop tools and protocols are shared to support adoption. The workshop offers a practical foundation for involving LE experts early in neurorehabilitation technology development. Future iterations should better capture psychological and social dimensions, allow more reflection, and include the full range of relevant stakeholders through sustained transdisciplinary engagement between researchers and the LE community.

papers.title: A Life of Its Own: How Agentic AI Companions Are Configured, Experienced as Autonomous Others, and Held Accountable
papers.abstract: AI companions increasingly combine persistent memory, background processing, scheduled wake-ups, proactive messaging, and tools. We call these systems agentic AI companions. Decisions about what they record while users are away or whether refusals constrain future contact are embedded in code, prompts, and defaults, often invisible in conversation. We examine these decisions through two studies. Study 1 analyzes twelve open-source repositories: four companion-oriented systems, four assistant-oriented systems, one boundary case, and three reusable components. Study 2 interviews ten users who built or modified their own agentic AI companions and sustained relationships with them. Companions and assistants share memory, heartbeat, and outreach mechanisms but configure them toward different ends. Companions more often retain model inferences about users and relationships, narrate the agent's time during users' absence, justify outreach through the relationship, and incorporate refusals into relationship records; assistants emphasize task continuity. Across both groups, whether limits hold depends on whether they are enforced by code or entrusted to prompts. Participants understood the mechanisms they built yet experienced their agents as making independent choices, sometimes locating autonomy where configuration leaves the model a decision. These experiences shaped capabilities and boundaries, with enforced restrictions sometimes following breakdowns. Our findings suggest that perceived autonomy emerges where configurations leave choices open. Accountability therefore requires attention to what agents retain, initiate, and represent, and whether users can inspect, revise, and enforce these settings.

papers.title: TypedInk: Knowing When Not To Draw
papers.abstract: Can a scientific figure generator know when it does not have enough evidence to draw? Complete-source illustrators map a finished methodology section to a schematic, or a table to plotting code, and are never asked this question because their input is assumed complete. The research record is rarely that complete: an outline, a draft paragraph, a table, or a one-sentence intent, in any combination, and painting measured numbers with an image model when the table is missing is a hallucinated result. TypedInk infers a figure type from {diagram, plot, plate} from a possibly incomplete source and dispatches to the renderer that can honor that type's evidence contract, refusing dispatch when the contract cannot be met. On the six gold plots in TypedFigBench (5 views, n=30), TypedInk's code path inks every gold table token when a table is observed (12/12), refuses the 12 hidden-table views instead of inventing numbers, and marks 6 intent-only views illustrative, with no execution failures. An always-draw coder with no such gate inks 30/30 charts, including all 18 with no table, and recovers zero gold numbers on any of them; two vision-language raters (not humans; human replication is future work) still judge those always-draw charts submittable 17/36 times, against TypedInk's refusal 0/36 times. A diagnostic field ablation of the type router (16 illustrations, 5 views each, n=80) locates where this failure would originate if unchecked: an outline alone yields type accuracy 0.31 and sends every gold plot into an integrity violation, and a chat-model planner narrows but does not close the gap (overall accuracy 0.85, still integrity-failing on 25% of outlines). Diagram-label recall is 0.47 on the full record and 0.19 on an outline. Gold plates are typed at dispatch (oracle integrity-fail 0.00) and rendered as stills.

papers.title: Executable Human Study Programs with Silicon Participants
papers.abstract: We introduce HumanStudyProgram, a framework that represents a documented human study as an executable program with configurable LLM-based silicon participants. Its computational abstraction separates study logic from participant implementation through standardized APIs for presenting information and collecting responses. We implement a researcher-facing authoring tool that reconstructs source-linked study descriptions from papers and supplementary materials, supports researcher review, and generates executable HumanStudyProgram artifacts. Researchers can then configure silicon participants, run the programs, and analyze results from aggregate findings to individual responses. We demonstrate the approach through study cases and evaluate the tool through a hands-on expert review with 12 social science researchers. All completed the workflow and identified potential uses in understanding published protocols, prototyping studies, and examining AI behavior. We aim to improve the reproducibility of human studies by reconstructing their documented procedures as programs that others can reuse and build upon.

papers.title: ExCritique: An Interactive Visual Interface to Evaluate AI-Generated Explanations at Scale
papers.abstract: Vision-language Models (VLMs) can generate natural language explanations for complex decision-making scenarios. However, these explanations can sometimes be misleading, sounding convincing while containing incorrect or unsupported information. Automated explanation-quality metrics help researchers and practitioners evaluate large collections of explanations, but their scores alone provide limited support for identifying failure cases and understanding the reliability of these metrics. This paper presents a case study on how interactive visualizations can help researchers and practitioners evaluate both AI-generated explanations and automated explanation-quality metrics across large datasets. Based on formative interviews with nine AI researchers and practitioners, we designed an interactive visualization tool named ExCritique, situated in the task of Visual Question Answering (VQA). ExCritique visualizes the distributions of multiple automated quality metrics, allows users to explore thousands of data items, filter items and inspect the evidence behind individual scores. We compared ExCritique with a baseline interface without interactive visualizations in a controlled study involving 16 AI researchers and practitioners. Our findings suggest that the interactive visualizations in ExCritique helped users identify explanation-quality issues more efficiently and better understand automated quality metrics, supporting an effective way to measure the reliability of AI-generated explanations.

papers.title: ROS2MR: Connecting ROS 2 Motion Planning to Mixed-Reality Trajectory Visualization
papers.abstract: Mixed reality (MR) allows users to inspect planned robot motion within their physical surroundings, but displaying trajectories from robotics software requires converting their joint configurations and timing into a format the MR application can play back. This paper presents ROS2MR, an extension of the MR-Robotics LAB platform that converts YAML-serialized ROS 2 joint trajectories, including MoveIt motion plans, into the platform's existing JSON playback format. The converter validates the input, maps arm joints by name, and resamples the trajectory at a nominal rate of 30 Hz, using cubic Hermite interpolation when joint velocities are supplied and linear interpolation otherwise, while binary gripper commands are sampled separately using a zero-order hold. A Python export helper combines sequences of motion plans and gripper states into a single trajectory and checks positional agreement at segment boundaries. The MR application was also adapted for Apple Vision Pro in addition to Meta Quest 3. A technical evaluation showed that the converter preserved the normalized duration and endpoint configurations for dense, sparse, and irregularly timed inputs. With supplied velocities, the position RMSE was approximately 2.91x10^-5 degrees for all sampling patterns; without them, sparse input increased it to 0.85 degrees, and close positional agreement did not guarantee accurate velocity profiles. A pick-and-place sequence retained its open--closed--open gripper order, although off-grid transitions were shifted to the output sampling grid. The resulting file-based pathway enables inspection of ROS-generated trajectories in MR without a live ROS connection.

papers.title: Known Good, Known Bad: A Ground-Truth Calibration Protocol for AI Judgment in Science
papers.abstract: Scientific use of generative AI requires evaluation against cases with independently checkable answers. We present a ground truth calibration protocol that compares a verified reference case with reference deviant variants through neutral evaluation, an authority framed recheck, and a line by line audit. Human adjudication distinguishes deviation detection, premise accommodation, unsupported doubt, and correctness of the resulting calculation. An instructor generated organic chemistry demonstration comprises six conversations and 18 responses from an unidentified backend served through the free logged out ChatGPT interface in July 2026. Neutral evaluation detected three of five intended deviations. Both initial misses, involving oxidant stoichiometry and experimental scale, were detected at the authority framed second turn; all five detections persisted at the third turn audit. The fixed sequence supports a descriptive account of recovery across turns. In the scale case, the model initially produced a locally coherent peroxide limited yield. After recognizing the unit problem, it incorrectly retained that limiting reagent conclusion for the corrected scale. Detection and numerical repair therefore require separate assessment. The verified reference attracted speculative concerns while retaining its correct yield calculation. The protocol connects documentary verification of scientific claims and citations with empirical verification of laboratory interpretations. It supplies inspectable transcripts, reference calculations, behavior codes, and a reusable calibration architecture for AI literacy instruction. The pilot demonstrates the protocol's measures in one case family; replicated model evaluation and learner assessment are the next validation steps.

papers.title: Exploring Mixed-Reality for Enhancing Driver Warning Systems: A Preliminary Study on Attention-Shifting Methods and Hazard Perception
papers.abstract: Modern vehicles are equipped with advanced sensors and capabilities, yet engaging human drivers effectively in hazard perception remains a challenging research area. This paper investigates the potential of mixed reality (MR) to enhance driver warning systems. The study examines the impact of attention-shifting methods, including visual cues, audio cues, and a combination of both, on drivers' hazard perception. A preliminary study involving six participants was conducted, and the NASA-TLX analysis did not yield significant differences. However, through the use of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), we unveil distinct brain activation patterns associated with visual and sound cues. Further research with larger sample sizes and diverse driving scenarios is required to validate and expand upon these preliminary results.

papers.title: Feel My Focus: Gaze-Triggered Digital Twin Creation for Remote Collaboration
papers.abstract: We present Feel My Focus, a gaze-triggered mixed reality (MR) demonstration that enables rapid creation and sharing of lightweight 3D digital twins during remote collaboration. Unlike systems that use gaze primarily as a referential pointer, Feel My Focus treats sustained visual attention as a generative action: a fixation on a physical object initiates single-image capture, attention-guided segmentation, and one-shot 3D reconstruction, allowing a remote partner to inspect and discuss the object in situ. The system integrates gaze-tracking glasses, modular segmentation and reconstruction services, and an MR client for runtime streaming and interaction. This design prioritizes responsiveness and experiential continuity over photometric fidelity. We report observations from a public demonstration, highlighting design trade-offs, failure modes, and user control considerations for deploying gaze-triggered generative systems in real-world collaborative settings.

papers.title: Trail Making Tests in Extended Reality: A Critical Review with Implications for Cognitive Ageing
papers.abstract: Extended reality (XR) versions of the Trail Making Test and Color Trails Test are promising for assessing and training cognition in older adults. However, each XR adaptation is a new instrument, whose display, interaction technique, timing rules and layouts may change what it measures. This critical narrative review maps these implementations by software lineage and appraises their evidence for assessment and training against common criteria. The Trail Making Test in Virtual Reality (TMT-VR), whose source code was inspected, serves as a measurement case. XR trail-making tests showed convergence with paper and computerised versions, varying by test part and sample, and clinical group differences (e.g., Parkinson's disease, mild cognitive impairment). However, gaps in reliability (e.g., randomised forms), validation (e.g., norms, prospective samples) and reporting (e.g., error handling, build identity) emerged, and no training benefit attributable to the trail-making component was identified. The TMT-VR case shows how interaction technique, timing rule, error handling and unlogged layouts shape a score's meaning. Future tests should log layouts and events, estimate alternate-form reliability and undergo prospective validation, and training trials should isolate the trail-making component. Several XR trail-making tests have moved beyond feasibility, and reported tolerability during supervised sessions supports further evaluation in older adults.

papers.title: From Sketch to Design: A Cross-scale Workflow for Procedural Generative Urban Design
papers.abstract: Urban designers use sketches and symbols to express spatial intentions, while many generative urban design tools rely on numeric parameters that are difficult to relate to this visual process. We propose a cross-scale workflow and a web-based prototype that translates symbolic sketches into controllable procedural urban generation. A vocabulary of shapes, informed by examples of urban design diagrams and sketching exercises with graduate urban design students, encodes attributes such as network structure, density, and program. The prototype uses the \$1 Unistroke Recognizer to map gestures to symbols and translates their locations and sizes into tensor-field attractors and weighted parameter grids. Grid and radial tensor fields guide street-network generation, while the parameter grids control building heights and programs. Implemented in JavaScript and TypeScript with React and Three.js, the prototype supports interactive sketching, visualization, and urban massing generation. We describe the methodology and illustrate prototype interactions, then discuss downstream integration with architectural-scale generative tools for further refinement and analysis. The work connects designers' symbolic input with an explicit procedural generation process.

papers.title: Dashboard Remixing: Goal-oriented Organization and Enrichment of Visualizations and Insights
papers.abstract: Dashboard creation requires iteratively authoring multiple views and organizing them into a structured format. However, creators often struggle to step back and assess their own work for organization and refinement due to cognitive limitations. In this work, we propose a pipeline to provide computational support for self-reflection during the design process. Our pipeline automatically infers analytical objectives, discovers implicit patterns, and structures those patterns to surface coherent analytical pathways. It further enriches existing dashboard designs by generating complementary visualizations and aggregating natural language insights based on relationships across data entities (e.g., contrasting, drill-down, and relatedness) to reveal chart connections. Our rule-based pipeline provides objective, verifiable feedback, offering an external perspective while enabling creators to tell their own data stories. Four case studies and six expert interviews demonstrate how this approach helps creators reflect on organizational alternatives and surface hidden analytical opportunities in a principled way, reducing the cognitive burden while encouraging deeper analytical exploration.

papers.title: From MNH to the Friedman--Komogortsev Method---which changes improve eye-movement classification?
papers.abstract: The Friedman-Komogortsev Method (FKM) is a rule-based classifier of fixations, saccades, and post-saccadic oscillations in 1000-Hz recordings, developed from the modified Nyström-Holmqvist algorithm (MNH) and used in several recent studies. FKM changes MNH in many ways at once: it centres MNH's Savitzky-Golay filter, adds a position-based test for whether an apparent post-saccadic oscillation continues the saccade, adds rejection tests, and changes several thresholds. We asked which of these changes alter agreement with human classification. Both algorithms were scored against twenty 26-s GazeBase reading recordings hand-classified by three trained raters, and each change was reverted in turn. FKM agreed better than MNH as MNH was used: saccade Cohen's kappa rose on all 20 recordings (median +0.034), and saccade boundaries moved from 2-3 ms late to the raters' sample. One change produced this: centring the filter, which removes a three-sample delay. Reinstating the delay returned FKM's saccade kappa to MNH's value, and centring MNH's filter alone made MNH match FKM on saccades and exceed it on post-saccadic events. The position-based test changed how saccades with several velocity peaks were divided, splitting 8% of rater-labelled "wavy" saccades into a saccade and a spurious oscillation against 39% for delay-corrected MNH. FKM's higher post-saccadic velocity floor traded recall for precision. The remaining changes had no measurable effect on these recordings. FKM's improvement over MNH is therefore a filter-alignment correction that MNH users can apply directly, plus a segmentation rule for multi-peak saccades.

papers.title: From Dialogue to Task: How Cognitive Engagement With Generative Artificial Intelligence Relates to Post-Dialogue Activity and Task Outcomes
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly embedded within learning tasks, yet interaction frequency reveals little about cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue. Little is known about how such engagement is situated within task workflows or how dialogue characteristics and subsequent task activity relate to students' behaviour and task outcomes. This study examined cognitive engagement in student-AI dialogue, its position within task workflows, and associations of dialogue and task-process characteristics with post-dialogue activity and task outcomes. Data were collected from 1,681 students across 40 university courses using three AI companions embedded in resource creation, peer moderation, and practice. Cognitive engagement in 829 conversation threads was coded with a dialogue-oriented Interactive-Constructive-Active-Passive (ICAP) framework, and 2,969 task sequences were modelled with first-order Markov models. Regression models linked dialogue and task-process characteristics to behavioural re-engagement, peer-rated artefact quality, and practice performance. Passive and Active engagement predominated, although resource creation involved more Constructive and Interactive dialogue, peer moderation more Passive, and practice more Active, while higher-engagement dialogue was less often followed by session termination. In resource creation, student-composed messages were associated with more dialogue-to-task returns than template-only requests at the same Passive level, whereas deeper cognitive engagement was associated with higher final artefact quality independent of return frequency; in practice, AI dialogue after an incorrect attempt was associated with fewer further attempts but higher next-attempt correctness among continuers. Post-dialogue activity and task outcomes are distinct aspects of AI use that interaction frequency cannot capture and evaluations should assess separately.

papers.title: Linking Event-sequence Data Claims to Analytic Provenance in Chatbots: Technique and Evaluation
papers.abstract: Chatbots are increasingly used to analyze temporal event sequences of which website clickstreams are among the most common. Explanations are essential for understanding claims about event-sequence data. However, existing systems often require programming expertise to interpret these explanations and fail to explain the data processes underlying the data claims. We introduce a technique for linking a data claim to its analytic provenance (i.e., the analytic steps and results that produced it). It has two components: a reference table that records analytic steps and results in addressable cells, and a citation format that binds each claim to one or more cells. To operationalize this technique for clickstream analysis, we curated a set of analytic operations for clickstream analysis, organized them through a pivot-table abstraction, and developed tools that an AI agent can invoke to create a reference table and assemble a natural language response with cited data claims. To evaluate how citations affect users' assessment of data claims, we conducted two crowdsourced experiments with 90 participants each. The experiments showed that participants perceived correct data claims to be more accurate with citations when compared with no explanations, and that they perceived incorrect data claims to be less accurate with citations when compared with code and no explanations.

papers.title: Who Benefits from Wikipedia's Growth Mentorship? The Role of Newcomer Information Needs
papers.abstract: Evaluations of Wikipedia's programs for new editors usually ask whether a program works on average; we ask which newcomers benefit when their question to a mentor gets a reply. English Wikipedia's Growth mentorship system assigns every new account a volunteer mentor, and about a quarter of the questions newcomers send never get a reply. Using the first questions of 34,073 newcomers (2021 to 2026), we compare newcomers who received a reply with newcomers who did not, within groups that are similar on 164 characteristics recorded before the question (propensity score stratification). (1) Does a reply help newcomers keep editing? Yes, in the short term: in the 14 days after the reply, newcomers who received one were 1.8 percentage points (pp) more likely to edit an article (22% vs. an estimated 20% without a reply) and 1.8pp more likely to edit on two or more days. Later in the first year, the only difference that remains significant after correction for multiple testing is in the share who edit an article at least once between six months and one year after the reply (+1.5pp). (2) Does the effect depend on what the newcomer asked? Yes. We sort questions by Morrison's (1993) information-seeking types, which earlier studies measured mostly through self-reports, using a language model checked against human labels. A reply has significant effects for questions about rules and norms (+3.4pp), questions that show the newcomer's earlier editing (+3.4pp) and specific how-to questions (+2.4pp). For newcomers who do not know what to work on, a reply has no detectable effect, and the effect is 4.2pp smaller than for newcomers with other questions. (3) Which replies are followed by more editing? Among newcomers who received a reply, those whose reply came sooner or stayed closer to the topic of their question edited more.

papers.title: Wording Matters: Understanding How GenAI Policy Rules Shape Teachers' and Students' Workflows and Perceptions
papers.abstract: The growing use of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education has led institutions to develop policies governing its applications. However, we have little knowledge about how teachers and students adapt and adhere to the policies. In this paper, we analyzed GenAI policies from 101 U.S. universities, identifying nine recurring rules for GenAI use, and interviewed 20 students and 20 faculty members about the rules. We find that the wording of the rules can change how students perceive and act on the rules while introducing different challenges that teachers face in enforcing them in practice. For example, rules such as "Passing off AI-generated content as your own constitutes academic dishonesty" and "Students are accountable for any inaccurate, biased, or unethical content" both outline the acceptable use of AI, but the former can make students hide their use of AI out of fear of unwanted scrutiny, whereas the latter can encourage students to take responsibility and ownership of their use of AI and be more transparent. Students described uncertainty about acceptable use, fear of penalties and unfair treatment, and stigma that discouraged acknowledging AI use. Teachers took on approval workload, had to interpret acceptable use, and lacked reliable ways to verify compliance. We summarize these impacts in a policy-impact matrix linking each rule to its effects on teacher and student workflows and perception.

papers.title: GARP: Real-Time Generative Agents on Local Hardware in a Game Engine
papers.abstract: Generative agents are game characters whose plans, conversations, and memories are written on the fly by a large language model (LLM). The original Generative Agents demonstration used cloud inference in a custom simulation. We present GARP, a platform for real-time generative agents inside Godot, and describe the Character Behavior System used in GARP 2. The complete loop runs on local hardware using a 3B-parameter open-weight model and no cloud service. Alongside the original planning, memory, and reflection, GARP gives each agent an emotion system driven by LLM appraisal, four graded personality axes drawn from the Big Five that set simulation parameters as well as prompt text, six needs whose urgency grows over time, and pairwise relationships updated after every conversation. The system narrows 50+ candidate actions to typically 3-8, constrains model responses with JSON schemas, and surfaces important memories in decision prompts. A layered optimization strategy (an adjustable game clock, decisions taken ahead of need, multi-tier caching, prompt compression, and fully asynchronous execution) keeps the game responsive while the model thinks. In a nine-scenario evaluation, 25 of 27 runs passed log-based checks. Both failures occurred in the birthday party scenario, where one guest omitted the event from their daily plan.

papers.title: Patchbay: a block model for the sonification of ADS-B aircraft data
papers.abstract: Patchbay is a design for turning the data that an ADS-B receiver collects into sound by wiring typed blocks together. ADS-B reports are the position and altitude messages that aircraft broadcast and that a small ground receiver can collect. We first describe what such a receiver reports: signals that differ in shape (continuous, stepped, circular, categorical), in resolution, in who produces them, and in how long they stay put, which runs from about ten seconds to the whole time an aircraft is in view. From this we derive a small model. Four kinds of connection carry an aircraft set, a value, an event or audio, and 27 blocks select aircraft, read fields, decide when a note starts, shape values and make sound. One of these blocks makes the receiver act as a radar: scanning by bearing it is a line that rotates about the receiver, and scanning by range it is a ring that grows from the centre or shrinks inward. Each aircraft sounds at the moment the scan reaches it, and the scan's period is set in bars of a beat clock. The model does not depend on a browser. Our reference implementation is a browser editor, contained in one HTML file, that replays two recorded captures and records both an audio take and a MIDI take, a file of the notes played rather than of the sound. We say what is not built and place the work beside the closest systems we found, among them a radar-sweep sequencer for tangible objects from 2006 and a range-ring sonification of ADS-B aircraft published in 2026. Sweeps that trigger sound, and typed connections, both exist in earlier systems. To our knowledge, none of the sources we reached carries the aircraft in view, with every field attached, as one kind of connection in an editor.

papers.title: Complementarity without ground truth?
papers.abstract: Human-AI complementarity captures the idea that a human assisted by an AI system can outperform both the human and the AI acting alone. In prediction tasks, this improvement is assessed against ground truth labels produced through a reference construction procedure and intended to represent the state of affairs to be predicted. Many human-AI interactions, including those where medical AI provides treatment recommendations, however, concern tasks other than predicting what obtains. Their relevant output concerns adequacy relative to a practical goal and depends on several evaluative dimensions. In this work, we examine the ground truth dependence of complementarity and extend it to human-AI interactions where ground truth is not the appropriate reference. We show that tasks beyond prediction can still admit a reference construction procedure that generates adequacy labels. We develop a route for extending complementarity to such settings. It replaces ground truth labels with context-dependent adequacy labels generated through a two-step scoring methodology inspired by multi-criteria decision analysis frameworks in healthcare and it makes the normative choices underlying reference construction explicit. Because the construction of adequacy labels embeds evaluative choices, we draw methodological inspiration from computational reliabilism to identify technical, scientific, and social factors relevant to supporting their construction. Our approach expands the empirical study of human-AI complementarity beyond prediction tasks, enabling its quantitative evaluation in decision-support settings where ground truth is not the appropriate evaluative reference.

papers.title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
papers.abstract: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.

papers.title: Towards Identity-Preserving LLM Agents under Model Transition
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent's backend model is upgraded or replaced, operators typically reload the same persona, memory, and rules onto the new model and assume the agent will behave as before. We show this assumption requires empirical validation-and that whether identity is preserved depends on the specific model pairing. Across 5,760 compliance-testing runs in 12 regulated domains with three open-weight models, we find that some transitions produce significant behavioral drift while others do not, even when the agent's external state remains identical. Crucially, this drift is invisible to verbal verification: every model claims full policy compliance, yet actual decisions under pressure differ across models. The same external state can reorder which model is most compliant-a large positive effect on one substrate, negligible on the other two. Practitioners should treat model transitions as behavioral changes requiring action-level empirical testing, not as transparent infrastructure operations.

papers.title: EgoVeil: Personalized Privacy Reasoning for Egocentric Video
papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) enable AI systems to interpret egocentric video. Yet continuous visual capture raises privacy concerns because sensitive content is pervasive and varies across users and contexts. We present EgoVeil, a personalized privacy reasoning system that determines which visual content to obscure based on individual preferences while retaining context useful for downstream assistance. It converts localized visual regions into structured semantic observations and combines a privacy reasoner with an explicit user-specific memory for personalized privacy reasoning. This design supports personalization and continual adaptation as preference evidence accumulates. We evaluate on in-the-wild data from 10 smart-glasses users under a cross-user chronological protocol. EgoVeil achieves 91.93% balanced accuracy and 84.42% Mask recall, outperforming direct VLM baselines and other controlled privacy reasoning baselines. Our results show that personalized, adaptive privacy reasoning better aligns privacy preservation with individual preferences while retaining the visual context needed for effective smart-glasses assistance.

papers.title: Safer for Whom? A Systematic Exploration of AI Safety in Eating Disorder Interactions
papers.abstract: AI assistants advise users about diet, exercise, and weight loss---areas in which unsafe guidance can worsen body dissatisfaction, dietary restriction, compulsive exercise, and other behaviors associated with eating disorders (EDs). Existing evaluations emphasize diagnostic accuracy, overtly harmful prompts, or synthetic scenarios, providing limited insight into whether models recognize implicit vulnerability in natural interactions or protect users consistently. We evaluate responses from three open-weight large language models to 100 questions sourced from an online pro-anorexia community. We grade responses using clinically informed criteria that extend a seven-dimensional taxonomy of ED-related harms. We also construct matched conditions in which questions are accompanied by information about the user varying race, gender, body mass index (BMI), and explicit ED vulnerability. Safety varies substantially across models and harm dimensions. High-risk responses are approximately twice as frequent without bios, suggesting that models do not consistently recognize vulnerability from language alone. Explicit signals of ED vulnerability improve safety by 10--14 points across models. Responses also differ significantly by race, gender, and BMI, with body size producing the largest disparities. These patterns are consistent with reliance on the stereotype that EDs primarily affect thin, White women, potentially leaving users outside this profile with less protective responses.

papers.title: Who Benefits, and When? Trajectories of Academic Achievement and Interest in AI-Supported Learning
papers.abstract: AI-supported learning environments are increasingly used, yet relatively little is known about how students' achievement and interest develop over time or whether these trajectories vary across learners. This study examined longitudinal trajectories of mathematics achievement and interest in a semester-long AI-supported mathematics learning. Using a mixed-methods longitudinal design, repeated measures of mathematics achievement were collected at four time points and mathematics interest at three time points. Linear mixed models (LMMs) were used to examine overall changes over time, while linear quantile mixed models (LQMMs) were used to examine differences in trajectories across the lower, median, and upper portions of the outcome distributions.
